content: Colorado Tick Fever (CTF), also known as Mountain tick fever, Mountain fever, or American mountain fever, is an acute viral infection caused by the Colorado tick fever virus (CTFV). This virus is transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected Rocky Mountain wood tick (Dermacentor andersoni). CTFV belongs to the genus Coltivirus and primarily infects hematopoietic cells, particularly erythrocytes. This explains its ability to be transmitted through blood-sucking ticks and, in rare cases, via blood transfusion. The disease is predominantly found in the western United States and Canada, especially in high-altitude regions such as Colorado and Idaho. The virus was first isolated from human blood in 1944. Structurally, the virus is approximately 80 nm in diameter, non-enveloped, and contains a double-stranded RNA genome of about 20,000 base pairs, divided into 12 segments (Seg-1 to Seg-12). Viral replication occurs in infected cells and is associated with cytoplasmic granular matrices. The presence of the virus in mature erythrocytes is thought to result from its replication in erythrocyte precursor cells in the bone marrow, followed by the maturation of these infected cells. Colorado tick fever is a rare disease, and its historical perspective is not well-documented. There is no established classification system for this condition. Pathophysiologically, CTFV is an Orbivirus or Coltivirus that chronically infects Rocky Mountain wood ticks. The virus primarily targets bone marrow cells, disrupting the development of certain blood cells. Transmission occurs through the bite of an infected tick. Differentiating Colorado tick fever from other diseases is essential, as its symptoms—fever, chills, headache, body aches, and rash—can mimic other tick-borne illnesses, particularly those caused by the Rickettsiae family. Misdiagnoses may include typhus, spotted fevers, and Ehrlichiosis. Recognizing the biphasic fever pattern characteristic of CTF is crucial for accurate diagnosis. Epidemiologically, Colorado tick fever is rare, with only 83 cases reported between 2002 and 2012. The disease is primarily confined to the Rocky Mountain states, with occasional cases reported elsewhere in the United States. Its incidence does not appear to be influenced by demographic factors or age. The Rocky Mountain wood tick is the primary vector, and being bitten in an endemic region increases the risk of infection. The natural history of Colorado tick fever involves an incubation period of 3 to 6 days, though it can extend up to 20 days. Patients typically experience a biphasic fever pattern, with an initial febrile phase lasting about three days, followed by a brief remission and a subsequent recurrence of fever for 1 to 3 days. The virus can persist in the bloodstream for up to 120 days, necessitating precautions to prevent transmission through blood donation. Initial symptoms include fever, chills, headache, retro-orbital pain, photophobia, myalgia, malaise, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and a flat or maculopapular rash. During the second phase, symptoms may intensify, and a high fever may return. Severe cases, particularly in children, may require hospitalization. Rare complications include aseptic meningitis, encephalitis, and hemorrhagic fever. The clinical presentation of Colorado tick fever includes a range of symptoms, with fever, chills, headache, body aches, and lethargy being the most common. Physical examination findings in the early stages may reveal fever, lethargy, and generalized weakness. The biphasic fever pattern is a hallmark feature of CTF and helps distinguish it from other tick-borne illnesses. Laboratory confirmation of Colorado tick fever involves a combination of tests. Immunofluorescence assay is the gold standard for diagnosis. Other diagnostic methods include complement fixation tests targeting viral components and acute and convalescent serology. Currently, there is no specific antiviral treatment for Colorado tick fever. Management is primarily supportive, with hospitalization required in severe cases.
